title: Pipelining Fundamentals
summary: The assembly-line idea that makes every modern CPU fast — why overlapping instruction stages raises throughput, not the speed of any single instruction.

slides.markdown:
**Pipelining** overlaps the stages of successive instructions the way a laundromat overlaps washing, drying, and folding for different loads of clothes — each machine works on a different load at the same time instead of sitting idle while one load finishes start to finish.

No single load gets done any faster. But loads finish one after another far more often, so the whole laundromat's throughput climbs. A CPU pipeline does exactly this with fetch, decode, and execute.

slides.subTitle: Overlapping independent stages
slides.markdown:
A non-pipelined CPU finishes instruction 1 completely — fetch through write-back — before instruction 2 even starts fetching. A pipelined CPU splits execution into stages built from **separate hardware**, so while instruction 1 decodes, instruction 2 can already be fetching.

This works because the stages use different resources at once: fetch reads instruction memory while decode reads registers. As long as two instructions aren't fighting over the same stage in the same cycle, they run **in flight together**, each at a different point in the pipeline.

slides.subTitle: Latency vs throughput
slides.markdown:
**Latency** is how long one instruction takes start to finish. **Throughput** is how many instructions complete per unit time. Pipelining trades a small amount of a single instruction's latency (each stage adds a little overhead for the pipeline register between stages) for a large gain in throughput.

An instruction still takes the same number of stages to fully complete — maybe even one cycle more, once you count the pipeline-register delay. What changes is that a *new* instruction finishes almost every single cycle once the pipeline is full, instead of only every several cycles.

slides.subTitle: The pipeline diagram
slides.markdown:
The standard way to read pipelined execution: instructions down the rows, cycles across the columns, each cell showing which stage that instruction occupies.

![Pipeline diagram showing four instructions overlapped across five stages and eight cycles](assets/pipeline-overlap-diagram.svg)

Read a **column** and every stage is busy on a different instruction — the overlap. Read a **row** for one instruction's march through the stages.

assets.alt: Pipeline diagram showing four instructions overlapped across five stages and eight cycles

slides.subTitle: Ideal speedup vs reality
slides.markdown:
With **N** pipeline stages and enough independent instructions to keep it full, the ideal speedup over non-pipelined execution approaches **N×** — an N-stage pipeline can have up to N instructions in flight simultaneously.

Real pipelines never hit this. Filling the pipeline takes N-1 cycles at the start, and every real program has **hazards** — cases where one instruction depends on another, or where a branch stalls the fetch of the next instruction — that force bubbles (idle cycles) into the pipeline. The rest of this group is about exactly those hazards and what hardware does about them.

slides.subTitle: "Pipelining makes my instruction faster"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If I pipeline the CPU, each instruction will complete faster."

**Why it's wrong:** pipelining adds register overhead between stages, so one instruction's latency is the same or slightly *longer* than single-cycle. Nothing speeds up any instruction's own journey through the hardware.

**Correct model:** pipelining raises **throughput** — instructions finished per second — by keeping stages busy on different instructions at once. One isolated instruction, alone, gets no benefit.
